clue.text: Recruitment consultant's savage job?

definitions.meaning: someone who poaches senior staff from rival firms for a client
read literally, the work of a tribesman who takes enemies' heads as trophies

explanation.surface: A wry question about what a recruiter actually does all day, as if the job were brutal.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is' and links the two senses: the modern business title and the old literal one.
explanation.definitionFit: Executive recruiters are commonly nicknamed after the trophy-collecting warriors because they hunt talented people for firms.

clue.text: Shoes almost ruined stockings

indicators.note: ruined footwear is knocked out of shape, so the remaining letters are rearranged
almost the whole word, so its final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Damaged footwear has spoiled someone's nylons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims Shoes to SHOE, and 'ruined' rearranges those four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Hose is an old collective term for stockings and tights, still used in hosiery.

clue.text: Deal set out about marathon, possibly, in Sussex town?

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go about, i.e. around, the other piece
set out in the sense of laid out afresh, so the letters of the word are rearranged

parts.note: a marathon is an example of a run, hence the 'possibly'

explanation.surface: Someone arranges a deal concerning a marathon held in a southern English town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set out' is the anagram signal and 'about' the container. Arundel is a castle town in West Sussex, southern England; Deal is itself a Kent town, a nice decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Arundel is a historic market town in West Sussex, famous for its castle.

clue.text: Mutineer hasn't broken emotional type of story

indicators.note: the mutineer's words are broken apart and reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A sailor in revolt has not yet cracked, in a tale meant to tug the heartstrings.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalists use this label for a feature focusing on personal experience and feelings rather than hard news.

clue.text: Raced up, considered, told a tale

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top, i.e. backwards

parts.note: raced means ran
considered, as in 'rated highly', means rated

explanation.surface: Someone dashed upstairs, thought it over, then spun a yarn.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'up' means read from the bottom, so the first synonym is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrate is to recount a story, so the past tense is a synonym for having recounted one.

clue.text: Changes in time to get into team on the up

indicators.note: the abbreviation has to get into the other piece, sitting inside it
in a down clue, on the up means the word is written upwards, i.e. reversed

parts.note: a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: A manager makes alterations so the time is right for a team on the rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the up' turns SIDE into EDIS, and 'to get into' puts T inside it: EDI-T-S.
explanation.definitionFit: Edits are revisions or alterations made to a text or recording.

clue.text: Old politician in hotel wearing toupee

indicators.note: the hairpiece is worn over the other letter, so that letter sits inside it

parts.note: a toupee is a small hairpiece, i.e. a wig
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A former MP is spotted in a hotel sporting a hairpiece.
explanation.definitionFit: The Whigs were a British party of the 17th to 19th centuries, forerunners of the Liberals.

clue.text: Farmers might combine for this

parts.note: combine looks like farmers teaming up, but it is the verb from the big farm machine that cuts and threshes grain in one pass

explanation.surface: Agricultural folk might join forces for some cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'combine' seems to mean cooperate; it is really the machine's work, reaping a crop.
explanation.definitionFit: Gathering in the year's crops is the job a combine harvester does, so farmers combine to bring it in.

clue.text: Ecofriendly sign somewhere hot

parts.note: environmentally friendly policies are called green
in astrology each of the twelve signs governs a house of the horoscope, so a sign can be a house

explanation.surface: An environmental symbol points to some warm place.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pulls 'Ecofriendly' and 'somewhere hot' towards global warming, but the answer is just a glass building for plants.
explanation.definitionFit: A glasshouse for plants is kept warm by trapped sunlight, making it a hot spot.

clue.text: Maiden after dancing must keep this to be quiet

indicators.note: the single letter comes after the rearranged word
dancing letters move about, so the word is rearranged

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A girl after a dance must keep something under wraps to stay silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dancing' signals the anagram. The definition works through the idiom 'keep stumm', British slang (from German) for saying nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom 'keep stumm' means to stay silent, so this word completes that phrase.

clue.text: Make stronger check on police, perhaps

parts.note: to check a horse is to rein it in
a police force is one example of a force, hence 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: Strengthen oversight of the constabulary.
explanation.definitionFit: To bolster or strengthen something, such as a wall or an argument, is to add support to it.

clue.text: True loner left in a muddle one could predict a lot

indicators.note: letters in a muddle are jumbled, so these three words are rearranged together

explanation.surface: A genuine solitary person left confused could foresee much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot' hints at a gambler's luck as well as quantity: this person predicts your lot, your fate.
explanation.definitionFit: A clairvoyant who reads palms or cards claims to foresee a client's fate, or lot.

clue.text: Cap supplier?

parts.note: a cap here is not a hat but a crown fitted over a damaged tooth

explanation.surface: Who provides headgear?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cap' suggests a hatter; the question mark warns of a dental crown instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist in operations on teeth fits crowns, known informally as caps, over damaged ones.

clue.text: A large Scot's cavorting, come what may

parts.note: large in stature means tall

indicators.note: cavorting means leaping about, so the letters of the word move into a new order

explanation.surface: A big Scotsman is prancing about whatever happens.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean regardless of the price or consequences, whatever happens.

clue.text: Skilful journalist following up story on books

indicators.note: in an across answer one piece on another sits just before it
the journalist's abbreviation follows up, coming after the rest

parts.note: a tale is a story
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible
ED is short for editor, the crossword's stock journalist

explanation.surface: A capable reporter chases a story about the publishing world.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone with natural ability and expertise.

clue.text: Precisely, I agree!

definitions.meaning: exactly arranged, neat and correct in every detail
an exclamation of assent, like 'quite right'

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means arranged exactly right, and is also said as a reply of hearty agreement.

clue.text: Talk about trendy doctor beginning to order a bit of the wet stuff

definitions.text: a bit of the wet stuff

indicators.note: the talking word goes about, i.e. around, the other pieces

parts.note: to rap is to talk, as in a rap session
something trendy is in

indicators.note: the beginning to the word, its first letter, is used

explanation.surface: A fashionable doctor discusses starting to sort out a spot of rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the talk word around the other three pieces, and 'beginning to' takes only the first letter of 'order'.
explanation.definitionFit: A single drop of rain is a tiny part of the wet weather.

clue.text: Spectacles no good for girls

indicators.note: no good means the abbreviation for good is taken away

parts.note: spectacles are glasses

explanation.surface: Eyewear is useless for young women.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasses is a northern British and Scottish word for young women.

clue.text: Reportedly glimpsed Apple's online assistant? That's magic!

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the words are spoken, so their sound gives the answer

parts.note: glimpsed is saw, and Apple's voice assistant is Siri, which said together in a British accent sound like the answer

explanation.surface: Someone claims to have spotted the iPhone's digital helper, and finds it wizardry.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent 'saw Siri' and the answer sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorcery is witchcraft or wizardry, the practice of magic.

clue.text: Unsupported, like a bed with just a mattress?

definitions.meaning: without foundation or evidence, as a claim can be

definitions.text: like a bed with just a mattress?
definitions.meaning: literally lacking the divan base that a mattress usually sits on

explanation.surface: A sleeping arrangement without a frame is left unpropped.
explanation.definitionFit: A groundless claim has no foundation, and a mattress on the floor literally lacks the bed base.

clue.text: Going to great lengths in the end

definitions.meaning: drastic, taking measures as far as they can go
situated at the very end or edge, as in the far north of a country

explanation.surface: Someone makes heroic efforts, eventually.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means both utmost or drastic and outermost, lying at the farthest point.

clue.text: Nerd soon crept out to find reporter

indicators.note: out in the sense of wrong or disordered, so the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A geek sneaked out early to track down a journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's foreign or political specialist who sends in stories is its correspondent.

clue.text: A bit of flower power — and the rest

parts.note: P is the symbol for power in physics
et al, Latin et alii, means and others

explanation.surface: A slogan of hippie flower power, plus everything else that went with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower power' looks like one phrase, but 'flower' belongs to the definition and 'power' to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Each coloured leaf of a bloom's corolla is one part of the flower.

clue.text: Little humour, it's said

indicators.note: it's said signals that the word is spoken, so a sound-alike gives the answer

parts.note: wit is clever humour

explanation.surface: Not much in the way of jokes, people say.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny amount, as in 'not a whit better', is a little.

clue.text: Periodical observer

definitions.meaning: a magazine published at intervals; a long-running British weekly

explanation.definitionFit: The Spectator is a British weekly political magazine, and a spectator is anyone watching; The Observer is also a paper, a neat decoy.

clue.text: Freeloader given shelter by companion

parts.note: the lee is the side sheltered from wind
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A sponger is taken in by a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasitic hanger-on who lives off others is likened to the bloodsucking worm.

clue.text: Island protected by whisky enthusiasts

indicators.note: the answer is protected by, i.e. held within, these neighbouring words

explanation.surface: A Hebridean isle guarded by lovers of Scotch.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is the largest of the Inner Hebrides, off Scotland's west coast.

clue.text: Place ideal to host university is tense

indicators.note: the outer pieces host, i.e. hold, the university letter inside

parts.note: PL is the abbreviation for Place in addresses
ideal means perfect

explanation.surface: An ideal location for a campus feels anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tense' looks like nervous, but it is the grammatical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The past perfect, as in 'had gone', is a verb tense in grammar.
